references.text: The eighth commandment in the Decalogue prohibits theft, which is the same prohibition that opens Leviticus 19:11.
Prohibition against spreading false rumors and giving false testimony, corresponding to the prohibition against lying to one's neighbor.
Repetition of the eighth commandment against theft in Deuteronomy's version of the Decalogue.
Warning against giving false testimony against one's neighbor, relating to the prohibition against lying.
Prayer to be kept away from lies and deceit, reflecting the ethical principles in Leviticus 19:11.
Prophetic accusation against those who steal, lie, and swear falsely, directly mirroring the prohibitions in Leviticus 19:11.
Hosea accuses Israel of lying and stealing, breaking the same commandments mentioned in Leviticus 19:11.
Exhortation not to think evil against one's neighbor and not to love a false oath, corresponding to the prohibitions against deceit and lying.
Jesus cites the commandment against theft as part of the way to eternal life, continuing with loving one's neighbor.
Paul summarizes the commandments, including the prohibition against theft, under the commandment to love one's neighbor.
Exhortation to put away lying and speak truth with one's neighbor, a direct New Testament parallel to the prohibition against lying to one's neighbor.
Exhortation to the thief to steal no longer, repeating the prohibition against theft.
Exhortation not to lie to one another, directly reflecting the prohibition against lying in Leviticus 19:11.
